concept.name: Terraform Modules & State

relationships.description: Connects Terraform Modules & State to canary deployments in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Terraform modules package reusable infrastructure patterns behind versioned input/output contracts, while the state file (`terraform.tfstate`) maps those HCL resource blocks to real cloud IDs. Treating state as a concurrency-locked, blast-radius-scoped database—never a shared monolith—is what keeps Infrastructure as Code safe at scale.
spark.keyTakeaway: Split state by environment and lifecycle tier, store it in encrypted remote backends with native locking, pin versioned modules, and use `for_each` instead of `count` to avoid accidental resource destruction.

concept.whyItMatters: A single misconfigured `terraform apply` against a monolithic state file can destroy a production RDS database or lock out an entire engineering org for hours. Clean module boundaries and isolated, locked remote state turn risky manual cloud clicks into repeatable, peer-reviewed changes.
whenToUse: Provisioning repeatable cloud foundations (VPCs, EKS/GKE clusters, IAM roles, RDS instances) across dev, staging, and production.
Platform teams exposing 'golden path' self-service modules with baked-in encryption, tagging, and security baselines.
Multi-engineer teams requiring atomic state locking, drift detection, and PR-based `terraform plan` previews.
whenNotToUse: Fast-changing application deployments (container image tags, Kubernetes Pods/Deployments)—use Helm, ArgoCD, or Flux instead of Terraform.
Putting 500+ unrelated resources (network + DB + 30 microservices) into one giant `terraform.tfstate`, making every `plan` take 15 minutes.
Ad-hoc one-off data migrations or imperative tasks better handled by scripts or Ansible.
keyPoints: **State is the source of truth for resource mapping**: `terraform.tfstate` links `aws_db_instance.main` to `arn:aws:rds:...` and caches attributes—never commit it to Git because it stores secrets in plaintext.
**Enforce remote state locking**: Use S3 (`use_lockfile = true` in Terraform 1.10+ or DynamoDB), GCS, or Terraform Cloud so two concurrent `apply` runs cannot corrupt state.
**Keep modules shallow and composable**: Pass dependencies via explicit inputs/outputs (composition) rather than nesting 5 levels of modules or abusing `terraform_remote_state`.
**Prefer `for_each` over `count`** for lists of resources: removing item `[0]` with `count` shifts every subsequent index and destroys/recreates unrelated resources.
**Use `moved` and `import` blocks (Terraform 1.5+)** to refactor module names or adopt existing cloud resources cleanly via PRs without `terraform state rm/mv` CLI surgery.

examples.title: Preventing Accidental RDS Destruction During Refactoring with `moved` Blocks
examples.scenario: An engineer renames `module.postgres` to `module.orders_db` inside a production Terraform root module. A naive `terraform plan` shows `1 to destroy (aws_db_instance), 1 to add`.
examples.outcome: Adding a `moved { from = module.postgres; to = module.orders_db }` block updates the state addresses in-place during `apply`, resulting in `0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy`.

examples.title: Cutting Plan Time from 11 Minutes to 25 Seconds via Layered State
examples.scenario: A 40-person team shared one 1,400-resource state file covering VPCs, EKS, and 25 app databases; every minor IAM tweak blocked all deploys behind a 11-minute state lock.
examples.outcome: Splitting into layered root modules (`01-network`, `02-platform-eks`, `03-app-rds` per env) isolated blast radius and dropped `plan` times to 15–30 seconds.

tradeOffs.factor: Monolithic State vs. Layered Root Modules
tradeOffs.pro: Monolithic state allows direct HCL references (`aws_vpc.main.id`) across all resources in one `apply`.
tradeOffs.con: Slow plans, huge blast radius, and frequent lock contention; layered states require reading outputs via SSM/data sources.

tradeOffs.factor: Git-Tag Pinned Modules vs. Local Relative Paths
tradeOffs.pro: Versioned registry/Git tags (`?ref=v2.4.0`) let dev adopt breaking module changes before prod.
tradeOffs.con: Local paths (`../modules/vpc`) force every environment onto the same module code simultaneously, risking prod breakage on refactor.

tradeOffs.factor: `terraform_remote_state` vs. Cloud Parameter Store / Data Sources
tradeOffs.pro: `terraform_remote_state` is built-in and requires zero extra AWS/GCP resources.
tradeOffs.con: Grants read access to the entire upstream state JSON (including secrets!) and tightly couples consumer directories to upstream output schemas.

failureModes.name: Concurrent Apply Without State Locking
failureModes.description: Two engineers or CI jobs run `terraform apply` simultaneously against an unlocked S3 bucket; the second write overwrites the first's newly created resources, orphaning live cloud infrastructure.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable `use_lockfile = true` (S3 native lock in Terraform 1.10+) or DynamoDB lock tables and run all applies strictly from serialized CI pipelines (Atlantis, Spacelift, GitHub Actions concurrency groups).

failureModes.name: Index-Shift Destruction from `count`
failureModes.description: Removing the first subnet or IAM user from a `list(string)` passed to `count = length(var.users)` shifts indices `1..N` down by one, forcing Terraform to destroy and recreate `N` live resources.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use `for_each = toset(var.users)` or `tomap(...)` so resources are keyed by stable string identifiers instead of integer array positions.

failureModes.name: Plaintext Secrets Exposed in `terraform.tfstate`
failureModes.description: Marking a variable `sensitive = true` hides it from CLI stdout, but `random_password`, `aws_db_instance.password`, and TLS private keys are still stored in plaintext inside the state JSON.
failureModes.mitigation: Encrypt state buckets with KMS, restrict IAM `s3:GetObject` strictly to CI runners, and prefer ephemeral write-only attributes (`password_wo` in Terraform 1.11+) or Secrets Manager generation.

failureModes.name: Manual Console Changes Causing Silent Drift
failureModes.description: An engineer emergency-edits a Security Group rule in the AWS Console; the next unrelated `terraform apply` silently reverts the rule back to the old HCL definition.
failureModes.mitigation: Run scheduled daily `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` drift-detection jobs and enforce read-only console access in production.

commonMistakes: Using `terraform.workspace` (`dev`/`prod`) with shared backend configs when environments have different architectures—prefer separate directories/root modules for prod isolation.
Leaving `terraform_remote_state` IAM permissions open to developers, exposing plaintext DB passwords stored in upstream state files.
Running `terraform apply -auto-approve` locally from laptops instead of reviewing `plan` output in a pull request.
Forgetting `prevent_destroy = true` lifecycle rules on stateful databases, KMS keys, and S3 buckets.
Hardcoding provider versions (`~> 5.0` vs unpinned) inconsistently without committing `.terraform.lock.hcl` to Git.

sections.content:
## The idea

Terraform is declarative: you describe *what* infrastructure should exist in HCL, and Terraform computes the DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) to reconcile current reality with your desired config. **Modules** provide abstraction and reuse—encapsulating a group of resources (e.g., a multi-AZ VPC with flow logs and NAT gateways) behind typed `variable` inputs and `output` values.

**State (`terraform.tfstate`)** is the bridge between abstract HCL names (`module.vpc.aws_subnet.private["us-east-1a"]`) and concrete cloud IDs (`subnet-0a1b2c3d`). Without state, Terraform wouldn't know which cloud resources it owns versus what was created elsewhere, nor could it detect deletions or compute minimal diffs without scanning every API in your AWS/GCP account.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider promoting a `v1.3.0` PostgreSQL module change through a layered CI/CD workflow:

1. **Module Authoring**: The platform team updates `terraform-aws-rds` (adding encrypted read-replica support), runs `terraform test` against an ephemeral sandbox, and tags `v1.3.0`.
2. **Root Module Update**: An app team bumps `source = "git::https://.../terraform-aws-rds.git?ref=v1.3.0"` in `envs/prod/orders-db/main.tf` and opens a PR.
3. **Locked Plan in CI**: GitHub Actions (with a per-directory `concurrency` group) acquires the S3/DynamoDB state lock (`LockID`), downloads `terraform.tfstate` (`serial: 42`), refreshes live AWS RDS attributes, and posts the exact diff (`~ update in-place`, `+1 read_replica`) on the PR.
4. **Serialized Apply**: After peer approval and merge, CI acquires the lock again, verifies the plan matches, creates the replica via AWS APIs, and writes `serial: 43` back to the KMS-encrypted S3 bucket before releasing the lock.
5. **Downstream Consumption**: The module writes the new read-replica endpoint to AWS SSM Parameter Store (`/prod/orders-db/ro_endpoint`), which the EKS app layer reads via `data "aws_ssm_parameter"`—avoiding `terraform_remote_state` coupling.

sections.content:
## Module boundaries, `for_each` & refactoring

Follow **flat module composition**: keep root modules as thin wiring layers that call 1–2-level-deep child modules (`network`, `eks`, `rds`) rather than deeply nested 'god modules' that hide 80 variables behind one giant abstraction. Every child module should expose narrow, strongly typed `variable` blocks with `validation {}` rules and `nullable = false` where appropriate.

When refactoring HCL names or importing legacy cloud resources, never edit `terraform.tfstate` by hand. Use declarative **`moved {}`** blocks to rename resource/module addresses safely in Git, and **`import {}`** blocks (available since Terraform 1.5) to generate HCL and adopt pre-existing cloud resources via standard PR review.

## Remote state & orchestration comparison

| Backend / Runner | Locking Mechanism | Secret Encryption | Multi-Env Isolation | Best Fit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **AWS S3 (`use_lockfile = true`, TF 1.10+)** | Native S3 conditional `If-None-Match` | SSE-KMS at rest | Separate state keys / buckets per tier | AWS teams wanting zero DynamoDB table overhead |
| **GCS Backend** | Native GCS object preconditions | CMEK / Google-managed | Bucket-per-env + IAM | GCP-native organizations |
| **HCP Terraform / Spacelift** | Built-in server lock + run queue | Encrypted + RBAC | Workspaces with policy (OPA/Sentinel) | Enterprise governance, drift detection, PR automation |
| **Atlantis (Self-Hosted)** | PR-level + backend lock | Depends on S3/GCS | Directory-based `atlantis.yaml` | Teams wanting GitOps `atlantis plan/apply` in GitHub/GitLab |

## Failure modes

**1. Partial Apply Leaving Tainted State**: An `apply` fails halfway through (e.g., IAM role created, RDS times out after 20 min). Terraform still saves the partial state up to the point of failure; re-running `apply` resumes from the checkpoint, though failed creation resources may be marked `tainted` for replacement.

**2. Circular Dependencies Between Root Modules**: Splitting `network` and `security` into two states fails if `network` needs an output from `security` and vice versa. Always enforce a strict acyclic dependency hierarchy (`00-org-iam` → `01-network` → `02-platform` → `03-apps`).

**3. State File Corruption from `-force-unlock`**: Running `terraform force-unlock` while a slow CI job is actually still applying causes two writers to race. Always verify in CI logs that the holding process is truly dead before unlocking.

## Protecting state secrets & stateful resources

Because `terraform.tfstate` stores sensitive outputs and resource attributes in plaintext JSON, treat the state bucket like a production database: enable **S3/GCS Object Versioning** (for instant rollback if state is corrupted), **KMS encryption**, and **strict IAM** (developers get read-only or PR-plan access; only the CI OIDC role can write state).

For irreversible resources (RDS instances, KMS keys, S3 data buckets), add `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` inside the module so any accidental deletion triggers an immediate hard error during `plan`.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Store all `terraform.tfstate` files in versioned, KMS-encrypted remote backends with locking enabled (never in Git).
- [ ] Split monolithic states into layered root modules by environment and change frequency (`network`, `platform`, `apps`).
- [ ] Pin module versions (`?ref=vX.Y.Z`) and commit `.terraform.lock.hcl` for deterministic provider binaries.
- [ ] Replace `count` with `for_each` on any resource list where items can be added or removed in the middle.
- [ ] Use declarative `moved` and `import` blocks in PRs instead of manual `terraform state mv/rm` commands.
- [ ] Add `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` to stateful databases, KMS keys, and production storage buckets.

interviewProblems.title: Terraform Modules & State
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Terraform Modules & State. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Terraform modules package reusable infrastructure patterns behind versioned input/output contracts, while the state file (`terraform.tfstate`) maps those HCL resource blocks to real cloud IDs. Treating state as a concurrency-locked, blast-radius-scoped database—never a shared monolith—is what keeps Infrastructure as Code safe at scale.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Remote State Backend applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Cloud Provider APIs.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Cloud Provider APIs experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Enable `use_lockfile = true` (S3 native lock in Terraform 1.10+) or DynamoDB lock tables and run all applies strictly from serialized CI pipelines (Atlantis, Spacelift, GitHub Actions concurrency groups).

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Split state by environment and lifecycle tier, store it in encrypted remote backends with native locking, pin versioned modules, and use `for_each` instead of `count` to avoid accidental resource destruction.
Avoid trap: Using `terraform.workspace` (`dev`/`prod`) with shared backend configs when environments have different architectures—prefer separate directories/root modules for prod isolation.
Avoid trap: Leaving `terraform_remote_state` IAM permissions open to developers, exposing plaintext DB passwords stored in upstream state files.
When to reach for it: Provisioning repeatable cloud foundations (VPCs, EKS/GKE clusters, IAM roles, RDS instances) across dev, staging, and production.
When to reach for it: Platform teams exposing 'golden path' self-service modules with baked-in encryption, tagging, and security baselines.

putItTogether.title: Putting Terraform Modules State Together
putItTogether.summary: Split state by environment and lifecycle tier, store it in encrypted remote backends with native locking, pin versioned modules, and use `for_each` instead of `count` to avoid accidental resource destruction.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Terraform Modules State before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Adding a `moved { from = module.postgres; to = module.orders_db }` block updates the state addresses in-place during `apply`, resulting in `0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy`.
